327 High Availability, Fault Tolerance, and Elasticity on AWS
11
AWS Networking, Part 2 –
Route 53 and CloudFront
When you type a URL into a web browser and are instantly presented with a website, what
happens behind the scenes is quite remarkable. The servers hosting these websites on the
Internet are accessible via a public IP address, which was discussed in Chapter 7. However,
what you enter into the browser's address bar is a domain name in Uniform Resource
Locator (URL) format—such as https://iaasacademy.com, a website I own and use to deliver
Cloud Computing courses.
The "magic" happens thanks to a service called the Domain Name System (DNS), which
translates URL-style domain names into their associated IP addresses. This translation allows
your browser to locate and connect to the correct server hosting the website you wish to
access. You can think of DNS as the Internet's phone book—designed to resolve human-
readable domain names into machine-readable IP addresses, enabling devices like your
desktop, laptop, or even smartphone to connect to the services provided by web servers
hosting a wide variety of websites and applications.
But DNS does more than map domain names to IP addresses. In this chapter, you will learn
how to scale your network architecture by integrating resources across multiple AWS regions
—a crucial strategy for organizations aiming to enhance global availability, performance, and
resilience. You will learn how Amazon Route 53, AWS's DNS service, can be used to implement
intelligent routing strategies across your globally distributed infrastructure. These routing
policies enable you to direct user traffic based on latency, geographic location, and health
checks, making them ideal for supporting multi-region deployments. Such configurations are
key to delivering low-latency access and establishing robust disaster recovery solutions.
In addition, this chapter introduces Amazon CloudFront, a globally distributed Content
Delivery Network (CDN) service. CloudFront accelerates the delivery of your content, such as
static assets, video streams, and APIs, by caching it at edge locations within the AWS Global
Infrastructure. This reduces the physical distance between your application and your users,
leading to lower latency and faster load times. By the end of the chapter, you will understand
how to architect applications that offer high availability and optimized performance to a
global user base.
The following topics are discussed in this chapter:

Understanding how Amazon CloudFront works
Amazon CloudFront idx_f8065513 is AWS's content delivery network service designed to distribute content
with low latency by leveraging the caching functionality of edge locations. The service uses
AWS edge locations and regional edge caches to route traffic over the AWS global backbone
network and store cached content closer to users.
CloudFront is optimized for delivering both static and dynamic content, such as documents,
images, and videos, to users. When a user requests content distributed via CloudFront, they are
routed to the nearest edge location with the lowest latency to retrieve the content as quickly as
possible. If the content is already cached at the edge location, it is delivered directly from there.
Otherwise, the request is forwarded over the AWS backbone network to the origin server (such
as an Application Load Balancer, Amazon EC2, or Amazon S3). The retrieved content is then
cached at the edge location for a idx_e65e7e31 specified Time to Live (TTL) duration.
Without CloudFront, requests travel over the standard public internet, encountering multiple
hops and routes, as illustrated in Figure 11.1:

331 AWS Networking, Part 2 – Route 53 and CloudFront
The following are some examples of use cases where you would benefit from using the Amazon
CloudFront service:
E-commerce website: An idx_d8178a0a e-commerce website can use Amazon CloudFront to
distribute product assets, such as images and descriptions, more quickly to end users
browsing the site. This improves the customer experience and helps keep users
engaged.
Online fitness app: An online fitness platform uses Amazon CloudFront to deliver
workout videos smoothly, ensuring uninterrupted playback even when thousands of
users are streaming during peak workout hours. Additionally, because videos are
cached at local edge locations, users don't need to retrieve the content from the origin
server each time, further improving performance.
Customize at the Edge: You can integrate CloudFront with Lambda (also known as
Lambda@Edge) to customize idx_ff185668 content delivery based on a variety of parameters. You
can also authenticate users at the edge, enabling faster logins and signups.
To use Amazon CloudFront, you create a distribution point, which defines your origin
endpoint. That origin can be an EC2 instance, a load balancer, an S3 bucket, etc. The
distribution point created using CloudFront is a special URL that you then give to your users
and takes the form of d123456abcdef8.cloudfront.net. Using this distribution point, users
are directed to an edge location closest to them and then routed to the origin over the AWS
backbone network, as illustrated in Figure 11.2.
Another critical edge service offered by AWS is Route 53, designed to help you configure DNS
settings essential for communication both within the VPC and externally on the public
Internet. Amazon Route 53 offers features such as routing policies and traffic shaping, which
you use to build resilient and highly available solutions across multiple regions. The next
section introduces you to this service.
Introducing Amazon Route 53, DNS, and routing
policies

Amazon Route 53 idx_86aeadcb is AWS's Domain Name System service, designed to translate human-
readable names into IP addresses that computers use to communicate over a network. When
you type https://iaasacademy.com in your browser window, you are directed to the IaaS
Academy training website. What happens behind the scenes is quite amazing. Figure 11.3
showcases a flowchart of the process:

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 332
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 332
Figure 11.3: Flowchart of DNS name resolution process
Here is a high-level overview idx_9b377d11 of the steps involved in DNS name resolution:
Your browser first checks its local cache to see if it already knows the IP address of the
IaaS Academy website. If it doesn't, it passes the request to the local operating system
cache.
If the name-to-IP address mapping is not cached (likely because you haven't visited the
website before), your browser sends the request to a DNS Resolver. This is a DNS server
that performs recursive queries on your behalf and is usually hosted by your local ISP,
although you may also use Google's DNS servers.
The DNS Resolver idx_cec2b208 then queries the root DNS servers to determine which top-level
domain (TLD) servers (.com) are responsible for iaasacademy.com
The root DNS servers do not store the IP address for iaasacademy.com. Instead, they
return the details (Name Server records and IP addresses) of the TLD servers for .com.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: 4.333 AWS Networking, Part 2 – Route 53 and CloudFront
chunks.sectionTitle: AWS Networking, Part 2 – Route 53 and CloudFront
chunks.content:
4.333 AWS Networking, Part 2 – Route 53 and CloudFront
The DNS Resolver then queries the .com TLD servers to find out which authoritative
name servers are responsible for iaasacademy.com
The TLD servers respond with the IP addresses of the authoritative DNS servers (Name
Servers) that host and manage the DNS records for iaasacademy.com. If you host your
domain name with Amazon Route 53, these would be the Route 53 name servers.
The DNS Resolver then sends the request to those authoritative servers and finally
obtains the IP address of iaasacademy.com
Your idx_e98e3809 browser receives the IP address and establishes a connection to the website,
allowing you to continue your training on AWS technologies
This entire process happens in just a few seconds over the public Internet. Furthermore, the
results are cached at the DNS Resolver, within your browser, and in your operating system,
ensuring that future requests are completed much faster.
Amazon Route 53 offers the following idx_c66dcb97 core services:
Domain registration
Creation and management of Hosting Zones
DNS Routing
Health Checks
Let's look at these in a bit more detail.
Domain Registration
Amazon Route 53 offers idx_6d79cb17 full domain name registration services that you can idx_0de19c8d use to purchase
your own domain names. When you purchase a domain name, you register it under a TLD such
as .com, .co.uk, .org, .in, etc.
Domain names are available on a first-come, first-served basis. This means that many common
names may already be taken by someone else, as each domain name must be unique on the
Internet.
As part of the registration process, you also select a lease duration for your domain name,
which can range from 1 to 10 years. You must renew this lease before it expires, or you risk
losing the domain to someone else. In fact, some businesses bulk-purchase popular names and
then resell or auction them at a much higher price.
Next, you will learn how to manage DNS records for your domain names using Hosted Zones.

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 334
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 334
Amazon Route 53 hosted zones
When you purchase a idx_b96f620a domain name with Route 53, you must create a hosted zone to manage
its idx_c39de57f records. A hosted zone is essentially a database, often called idx_f376b56f a zone file, that contains all the
resource records you define for your domain name.
Here are some common record types you can create:
Record Type Description
A/AAAA Records
Map a name to an IP address. For example, www.example.com →
w.x.y.z. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address, whereas an AAAA
record maps it to an IPv6 address.
CNAME Records
Canonical name records map one name (alias) to another name. For
example, you could map blog.example.com to www.example.com so
that both resolve to the same resource.
MX records Mail exchange records point to mail servers that handle email traffic.
Table 11.1: Example of DNS records
With Route 53, you can create two types of hosted zones:
Public Hosted Zones: Define idx_fdc67a0f how you want to route traffic for your idx_7344bff1 domain across the
public Internet. For example, instead of giving users the Amazon S3 static website
endpoint (http://belly-brew-coming-soon.s3-website-us-
east-1.amazonaws.com/), you can create a DNS record in Route 53 that points a
friendly domain name like bellybrew.co.uk to the S3 bucket. This makes it much
easier for users to remember and access your site.
Private Hosted Zones: Define idx_c99eac4c how you want to route idx_ba9cca9c traffic within private networks,
such as one or more VPCs. For example, you could use devserver.example.com to
point to the private IP address of an EC2 instance in a VPC.
Hosted zones enable you to define DNS records for specific domain names as well as create
routing policies for how traffic is directed to the resources that will host your application.
Depending on the type of traffic and protocol used to connect to your application, you will
need to create the appropriate record type. In addition to standard DNS records, as depicted in
Table 11.1, AWS also offers the option to create alias records, which are used to route traffic to
AWS-specific resources. This is discussed next.
•
•
335 AWS Networking, Part 2 – Route 53 and CloudFront
Alias records
In addition to standard idx_edee3b39 DNS records, Route 53 idx_06850b59 supports alias records, which are designed to
map your domain directly to specific AWS resource endpoints, such as:
An Application Load Balancer
An Amazon S3 bucket configured for static website hosting
An Amazon CloudFront distribution
Alias records are especially useful for mapping idx_286c1fab the zone apex (the root domain, without a
hostname). For example, the zone apex of www.iaasacademy.com is simply iaasacademy.com.
This allows you to use branded, corporate DNS names directly with AWS resources.

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 334
chunks.content:
In the next section, you will learn more about Amazon Route 53 routing policies, which can be
used to build global network routing with options for resilience and reduced latency.
Amazon Route 53 routing policies
Amazon Route 53 provides idx_eb8d2868 several routing policies that let you define how traffic is idx_a5a9923f directed to
your resources. These policies allow you to split traffic between multiple resources, improve
performance by routing users to the lowest-latency endpoints, or configure active-passive
failover solutions for high availability.
The main routing policies are:
Simple Routing Policy: The most idx_8277a256 basic policy. You define one record per DNS name,
but that record can point to multiple resources. For example, you idx_05cf34ca could map
www.iaasacademy.com to several EC2 instances with different public IP addresses.
Route 53 returns all available IP addresses to the client, which will then randomly
select one to connect to.
Failover Routing Policy: This idx_b12ea6e8 policy enables an active-passive setup. You idx_03b89708 designate
one resource as primary and another as secondary. Health checks monitor the primary
resource, and if it fails, Route 53 automatically routes traffic to the secondary resource.
This is particularly useful for ensuring resilience against Availability Zone or Regional
outages.
Geolocation Routing Policy: Routes traffic based on the geographical location of your
users. For idx_ad1d1bdc example, visitors from France can be directed to idx_723bef1d resources in the Paris
Region, while visitors from the UK are directed to resources in the London Region.
Latency Routing Policy: Routes idx_224c2d53 traffic to the resource that offers the lowest latency
from the user's location. This is commonly idx_78561636 used when you have copies of your website
deployed in multiple AWS Regions and want each user to connect to the fastest one.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 336
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 336
Weighted Routing Policy: Splits traffic between multiple resources based on weight
values you idx_c3d0cd38 assign. For example, if you deploy a new version of your idx_3f365680 application, you
might send 10% of traffic to the new resource and 90% to the existing one. Over time,
as you gain confidence, you can gradually shift all traffic to the new version.
Geoproximity routing policy: This policy idx_1fab63a7 lets you send users to resources idx_f0204d08 that are
closest to them geographically. You can also manually adjust the traffic distribution
using what is known as bias. For example:
If you want to send more traffic to your U.S. servers, you can increase the bias for
that region.
If you want to send less traffic to Europe (such as during maintenance), you can
decrease the bias for Europe.
This policy type is used to steer traffic between regions depending on location and your
chosen settings. You shift more or less traffic to a resource by adjusting the bias value.
Amazon Route 53 also allows you to perform health checks against your resources. Certain
routing policies, like the failover routing policy, will send traffic based on the results of those
health checks. Health checks are discussed next.
Amazon Route 53 health checks
Amazon Route 53 includes a health idx_7653ab2b check feature that ensures traffic is only routed to resources
idx_4346ddf1 and endpoints that respond as healthy. By default, Route 53 checks the health of your resources
every 30 seconds, but you can reduce this to every 10 seconds at an additional cost.
The health checking service helps you detect unhealthy resources and can redirect traffic to
other healthy resources, both within and across regions. This supports high availability and
service continuity. For example, if you configure a failover routing policy between a primary
site and a secondary site, you must set up health checks to monitor the primary site. If the
primary site goes down, Route 53 automatically directs customer requests to the secondary
site.
There are three types of health checks you can configure:
Health checks to monitor an endpoint: These checks the health of resources such as
an Application Load Balancer or the IP address of an EC2 instance.
Health checks to monitor other health checks: This groups multiple health checks
and evaluates the overall health based on a minimum number of healthy responses. If
•
•
◦
◦

the number of healthy resources falls below your defined threshold, Route 53 can act
(e.g., rerouting traffic).
Health checks to monitor CloudWatch alarms: You can create health checks that
follow CloudWatch alarms. For example, you might set up an alarm to trigger if the
number of EC2 instances behind a load balancer falls below a set value. If the alarm is

Amazon CloudFront, in this idx_8c6b269a example, is being used to cache content such as images and idx_ddd9e81e videos
locally at Edge Location, vastly improving the user experience. It also increases your web
application's reliability due to its globally distributed collection of edge locations. This not
only improves transfer speeds and lowers latency but also improves availability due to its
caching capability.
Another service that AWS offers, which improves the performance and availability of
applications by using the AWS global network to route user traffic, is the AWS Global
Accelerator. This service is discussed in the next section.
Introducing AWS Global Accelerator
The idx_0599ddaa AWS Global Accelerator is a network service designed to provide better network
performance to your application for your global users. The service improves the availability of
your application by directing your users' traffic through the AWS backbone network via an
edge location closest to them, thereby reducing latency.
The Global Accelerator allows you to assign two anycast IPv4 addresses that act as fixed entry
points for your application endpoints, which could be Network Load Balancers, Application
Load Balancers, Amazon EC2 instances, or Elastic IP addresses. You associate these IP
addresses with multiple endpoints in one or more regions. Users who connect to those
addresses are then routed via the endpoint that is most optimal in terms of location, latency,
and health.
An anycast IP address is one that is shared between multiple servers and locations, but traffic is
routed via the closest edge location in terms of network hops/latency. For example, if an
anycast IP address is associated with a service that needs to be made available in London as
well as Tokyo, a user in Tokyo will connect to the Tokyo network service, not London, avoiding
unnecessary latency over the public Internet.
Do not confuse the idx_cf6aaec8 Global Accelerator with Amazon CloudFront. The Global Accelerator is
designed to improve network performance and route traffic to application endpoints. In
contrast, Amazon CloudFront is a content distribution solution designed to cache content
closer to the end user.
In the next section, you will have the opportunity to complete a lab exercise where you will
implement a CloudFront distribution for the Belly Brew Co. Limited 'Coming soon' website.

Summary
This chapter explained how Amazon Route 53 and Amazon CloudFront work together to
improve website performance, resilience, and global distribution. Route 53 provides you with
the ability to register your company's domain names, perform DNS resolution, map human-
friendly domain names to IP addresses, and support advanced routing policies such as failover,
latency-based, and weighted routing policies.
Organizations use these services and features to build highly available and fault-tolerant
systems that automatically reroute users to healthy or geographically closer resources. Another
key edge service offered by AWS is Amazon CloudFront. This acts as a global Content Delivery
Network (CDN), caching content at AWS edge locations to minimize latency and accelerate
content delivery. Combined with health checks and integration options such as
Lambda@Edge, these services form the foundation for building scalable, secure, and high-
performance applications for worldwide users.
For Belly Brew Co. Limited, you discovered how these AWS services can help deliver their
website and digital content with faster load times and greater resilience, improving your
customer experience and engagement. By serving their "Coming Soon" site through
CloudFront, Belly Brew Co. Limited ensures that global visitors encounter minimal delays
regardless of their location, while Route 53 allows them to use a friendly domain name (e.g.,
bellybrew.co.uk) instead of a raw S3 bucket address.
As their business grows, they can also adopt routing policies for disaster recovery or expand
into multi-region deployments to serve customers across the U.K. and beyond. Ultimately,
these services give Belly Brew Co. Limited the technical backbone to build an engaging, reliable
online platform to support their brand growth and customer base.
The next chapter introduces you to Application Integration services on AWS. These services are
designed to help you design and build different architectural patterns for your applications
depending on their use case. You will learn about monolithic, microservices, and event-driven
architectures, which are important topics for the AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner exam.

Services
The third part focuses on building real-world solutions that align with architectural best
practices, such as decoupling application components and implementing integration patterns
that enable functions to be separated and scaled independently. These include queuing
services like Amazon SQS, notification services such as Amazon SNS, and event-driven
architectures. This approach helps avoid monolithic design patterns, where tightly coupled
dependencies can lead to widespread outages and a poor customer experience, particularly in
complex application workflows.
This section also introduces data analytics, machine learning, and artificial intelligence
services, enabling you to work with business data without worrying about the underlying
infrastructure. These fully managed SaaS offerings allow you to focus on building innovative
applications faster and more efficiently while reducing operational overhead.

12
Application Integration
There are three main architectural patterns when designing your applications: monolithic,
microservices, and event-driven. Recall the project you designed and built for Belly Brew Co.
Limited in Chapter 9. What you designed and deployed was a monolithic architecture. The
application consisted of a front-end user interface that allowed members of the public to
submit their email addresses on a sign-up form. The backend would process that data and
update the Amazon RDS database with the user's contact details. The same application would
then generate a presigned URL to email across to the user, so that they could download the free
recipe eBook.
Although the architecture comprised several isolated components like the Amazon RDS
database and Amazon SES to handle mass email messaging, the application itself runs as a
single unit on the EC2 instances you deployed in your VPC. While this monolithic architecture
has the advantage of being simple to develop and deploy, suitable for small applications, it is
difficult to scale specific parts of the application independently and is harder to update and
maintain. Sure, you have deployed the same application across multiple EC2 instances, across
multiple AZs, offering high availability. Nevertheless, with this type of architecture, any
component failure is likely to bring down the entire application stack.
In this chapter, you will learn why decoupling your application from traditional monolithic
structures reduces the impact when making component changes, ensuring that updates and
upgrades to new features can be released faster and with minimal impact.
You will learn how designing your applications as microservices, which involves breaking an
application into smaller, independent services that each perform a specific business function,
results in a more agile architecture. You will also learn about event-driven architectures, which
is where applications are designed to react to events asynchronously, such as when someone
places an order or there is a system update. Event-driven architectures improve scalability,
reduce dependencies between services, and support real-time processing.
The following topics are discussed in this chapter:
Understanding the application of notification services with Amazon SNS
Decoupling your application architecture with Amazon SQS and Amazon MQ
Designing event-driven workflows using the Amazon EventBridge services
Visualizing and architecting application components using Amazon Step Functions
Understanding the application of notification
services with Amazon SNS
Amazon Simple Notification Services (Amazon SNS) is a idx_812516ef push-based notification service idx_3393b2b9
that follows a publisher–subscriber (pub/sub) model. In this model, a publisher sends

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 14, Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence
chunks.content:
messages to subscribers via a central channel called idx_4eea4e9e a Topic. With Amazon SNS, one
component of an application can notify other components when an event or action occurs. The
subscribing components can then process the message and take appropriate action. Messages
are pushed directly to subscribers via a Topic and are not temporarily stored; however, retries
can be configured to ensure messages are successfully delivered to subscribing components.
Amazon SNS idx_b3ad0eae allows you to design a message notification feature for your application that can
handle high throughput, many-to-many messaging between distributed systems,
microservices, and event-driven architectures.
For example, suppose you want to be notified if your IAM users delete sensitive data stored in a
specific Amazon S3 bucket. To achieve this, you can create an event notification on the bucket
to send an alert when the event type s3:ObjectRemoved:Delete occurs. In this example, the
subscriber could be the email address of an administrator or the bucket owner. This type of
messaging is known idx_57f6e776 as Application-to-Person (A2P).
In another example, you can configure an Amazon S3 bucket to host images that end users
upload. Each time a new image is uploaded, an s3:ObjectCreated:* event occurs. You can
configure Amazon SNS to send a notification of this event to a Topic. A Lambda function can
then subscribe to this Topic, triggering it to process the image, such as adding a watermark.
This type of messaging is known idx_e3d5a081 as Application-to-Application (A2A).
When using Amazon SNS, your subscribers must be a supported endpoint type, which is
depicted in Figure 12.1:
•
•
•
•

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 352
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 352
Figure 12.1: SNS endpoints and supported protocols
Amazon SNS A2A endpoints include idx_271c0bb8 Amazon SQS, HTTP/S endpoints, AWS Lambda, and
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose. Data from Kinesis Firehose can then be offloaded and stored in
Amazon S3, Redshift, or other third-party services. You will learn more about Amazon Kinesis
in Chapter 13.
Amazon SNS A2P endpoints include idx_ab1daaaf email, mobile text messaging, and mobile push
endpoints.
Amazon SNS can send messages to multiple endpoints in parallel. This process is known as
fanout processing, which is idx_4dc5f35d discussed in the next section.
Amazon SNS fan-out scenario
Amazon SNS is idx_4a0f7ec7 designed to send out notifications to multiple subscribing endpoints in parallel
via topics. This means multiple components of your application process the same notification
for their specific functions as part of the overall architectural design. For example, in Figure
353 Application Integration
12.2, a notification or an order placed on an e-commerce website is being sent in parallel to
multiple endpoints.
Figure 12.2: Amazon SNS fan-out scenario
Upon placing a successful order via the application, a new order notification is sent to the
Amazon SNS NewOrderTopic. That notification is then pushed out to the following endpoints:
The SQS Queue is used to host details of a new order so that a backend component can
then retrieve the information and update the inventory system
A Lambda function may subscribe to the topic so that each time a new order is placed,
it triggers a shipping workflow in the shipping component of the application
An email endpoint is used to inform the customer that the order has now been
dispatched to them
Each system can operate independently, and all systems receive the message at the same time
in a fan-out architecture.
While Amazon SNS is a idx_f779a93d push-based notification system, sometimes you need a queuing
solution to hold messages so that backend components can process them as and when they are
ready. This further decouples your architecture stack and lends itself well to a microservices
design architecture. The next section introduces you to the Amazon Simple Queue Service
(Amazon SQS), which idx_56275f00 offers such a queuing solution.
•
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 12 354
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 354
Decoupling your application architecture with
Amazon SQS and Amazon MQ
Amazon SQS is a fully idx_ff217b8f managed message queuing service designed to help you build decoupled
architectures on AWS. With Amazon SQS, you can build distributed systems that lend
themselves well to a microservices architecture, where each component works independently
of the others. Using a queuing mechanism, one component of your application (such as the
frontend) can submit requests or tasks to a queue that other components (such as the
backend) can fetch and process whenever there is available capacity. This means that each
component can scale independently, and updates or upgrades can be released for each
component without affecting the others in the application.
Figure 12.3 shows an example of a idx_e965c52d media transcoding application that uses both Amazon SNS
and Amazon SQS to process videos idx_fe870f7c uploaded by end users.
Figure 12.3: Amazon SNS fan-out scenario
It uses a frontend user interface to enable uploads and backend instances to process those
video files. The application converts the raw video files into various formats and resolution
sizes. Each layer of the application stack (frontend and backend) can scale independently. For
example, the frontend scales based on metrics such as CPU utilization, while the backend
scales based on the number of messages held in the Amazon SQS queue.
If the frontend experiences many requests, resulting in CPU utilization rising above a specified
threshold, the Auto Scaling service deploys additional instances. Similarly, if the number of
355 Application Integration
messages in the Amazon SQS queue rises above a given threshold, the backend EC2 instances
scale out to accommodate demand and avoid extensive delays in processing requests.
Here is a breakdown of idx_60f48a1e the application workflow:
Users upload their video files using a frontend user interface hosted as a website on a
fleet of EC2 instances running in an Auto Scaling group
The videos are uploaded to a master Amazon S3 bucket, which generates a
CreateObject event that triggers a notification message to an Amazon SNS topic
Simultaneously, the SNS topic has multiple Amazon SQS subscribers – one for each
video format and resolution size. The messages are pushed forward by the SNS topic to
these SQS Queues
The SQS queues will host these messages for a default period of up to 4 days, which can
be increased to a maximum of 14 days
The relevant backend fleets of EC2 instances will regularly poll the queue they have
been configured to access and pull those messages. The application will then be able to
retrieve the relevant videos from the master Amazon S3 bucket.
The app servers will convert those videos into the required format and resolution and upload

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 354
chunks.content:
them to the transcoded S3 bucket as depicted in the diagram. The use of Amazon SQS queues
ensures that messages can be held in the queue for a period until the backend resources have
capacity to process those videos and reformat them. The frontend website does not need to
depend on the availability of the backend application servers in this design configuration,
offering a decoupled architecture for your application.
Next, you learn more about the types of Amazon SQS queues you can configure and their key
features.
Types of Amazon SQS queues
Amazon SQS offers two types of queues: Standard queues and First In First Out (FIFO)
queues.
Amazon SQS standard queues
Amazon SQS idx_2657c2fb Standard queues are designed to handle a nearly unlimited number of API calls
per second, and messages are delivered at least once. Because of the distributed nature of the
queuing system, your application must be able to handle duplicate copies of a message being
delivered. In addition, messages may not be delivered in the same order in which they were
added to the queue. So, your application should also be able to handle messages that are out of
order. The benefit of this design is that the service can scale to support very high transaction
volumes.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 356
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 356
Standard queues are useful when you need to process a very high number of transactions per
second. However, there is a quota on the number of in-flight messages for a standard queue. A
common example of using a standard queue is processing a large volume of credit card
validation requests for an e-commerce application.
Amazon SQS FIFO queues
Amazon idx_f3a77969 SQS FIFO queues preserve the exact order of messages. With FIFO queues, messages
are processed exactly once, and duplicates are not introduced. The trade-off is that throughput
is limited to 300 transactions per second, or up to 3,000 transactions per second if you use
batching (10 messages per batch). FIFO queues are ideal when the order of events must be
preserved and duplicates cannot be tolerated.
Here is a simple use case for an Amazon SQS FIFO queue:
Let's consider the case of online movie ticket booking. When you're buying movie tickets
online, requests need to be handled in the order they come in. For example:
At 10:01 AM, Person A tries to book Seat 12 and completes the payment
At 10:02 AM, Person B also tries to book the same seat and attempts payment
Without FIFO handling, person B might get the seat even though person A was successful in
completing the transaction 1 second earlier.
With an SQS idx_4791bf7f FIFO queue, the system processes Person A's request first, completes the booking,
and only then moves on to Person B. This ensures the seat goes to the person who booked it
first, keeping things fair and preventing double bookings.
While Amazon SQS is a queuing system native to the AWS platform, many organizations use
other message brokering services, such as Apache ActiveMQ, for their on-premises application.
Companies that wish to migrate their applications to the cloud can use the Amazon MQ service
for easier migrations. Amazon MQ is discussed in the next section.
Introduction to Amazon MQ
Amazon MQ is a idx_841d4bb5 managed message broker service designed to help application components
communicate and exchange information. It enables different services to talk to each other
directly, even if they are written in different programming languages or run on different
platforms.
Many organizations already use message brokers within their on-premises environments to
support existing applications. A common example idx_8b2d3c4c is Apache ActiveMQ, a popular Java-based
message broker.
•
•
357 Application Integration
When clients migrate their on-premises applications to the cloud, they may prefer to continue
using services that are compatible with existing third-party brokers instead of re-architecting
their applications for idx_164e6385 Amazon SQS. That's where Amazon idx_6dd37622 MQ fits in — it offers compatibility
with industry-standard APIs such idx_b3018784 as JMS (Java Message Service) and protocols idx_4f41f251 including

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 356
chunks.content:
AMQP 1.0 (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol), MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry
Transport), OpenWire, and STOMP (Simple Text Oriented Message Protocol).
Amazon MQ idx_8295506d is ideal when you simply want to perform a lift-and-shift migration of existing
legacy or on-premises applications that rely on existing broker protocols and APIs.
In the next section, you will learn about event-driven architectures that enable services to react
asynchronously to events, reducing tight coupling and improving scalability, flexibility, and
real-time responsiveness.
Designing event-driven workflows using Amazon
EventBridge services
Amazon EventBridge is a idx_e6235569 fully managed event bus service that can be used to route real-time
events from one application component to another. The targets of these events can include
AWS Lambda, Amazon Kinesis, HTTP/S endpoints, Amazon SQS queues, Amazon SNS topics,
and more.
With Amazon EventBridge, you can create an application architecture that reacts to events
from upstream components, ensuring that resources are only consumed when those events
occur. This has the added benefit of reducing overall costs. For example, you can invoke a
Lambda function only when an idx_deea75d7 event occurs, rather than running an EC2 instance hosting a
backend application that sits idle and incurs unnecessary costs.
Events can be system events, such idx_df340014 as an EC2 instance changing state from running to stopped,
or application events, such idx_455523aa as when a user uploads a video to an Amazon S3 bucket.
With EventBridge, you define rules that idx_060be485 specify matching patterns for incoming events. When
a matching event occurs, the rule sends the event to a target for further processing. For
example, Figure 12.4 depicts monitoring an EC2 instance state change.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: Chapter 12 358
chunks.content:
Chapter 12 358
Figure 12.4: Amazon EventBridge
As depicted in Figure 12.4, the following steps represent the workflow:
An EC2 instance idx_95b4a52b changes state idx_2cc7f6e1 from running to stopped (and vice versa)
These events are recorded in an event stream using the default event bus, which is
available in your AWS account. You can also create custom event buses for custom
applications.
A rule allows you to match an event to a target for processing. In this example, the rule
is configured to filter events where the EC2 instance state changes from running to
stopped.
The rule then sends the event notification to an Amazon SNS topic, which has an email
subscriber (such as an administrator) who needs to be notified whenever an EC2
instance is stopped
In addition to monitoring real-time events, you can also schedule EventBridge rules to trigger
events at designated times during the day, week, or month, or by using a rate expression. For
example, you could configure a Lambda function to run every 10 minutes.
A common use case for this is configuring EventBridge to trigger a Lambda function that stops
all development EC2 instances at 6 PM on weekdays after copying all log files, and then restarts
them at 8 AM the following weekday.

chunks.title: awscertifiedcloudpractitionerclf-c02certificationguidesecondeditio
chunks.heading: 4.359 Application Integration
chunks.content:
4.359 Application Integration
This helps reduce costs, especially if the development servers are running on On-Demand EC2
instances, where you idx_183cb06c are charged by the second when the instance is in the running state.
Building a distributed application often involves designing a workflow that invokes and
triggers various components. Often, you need to define this workflow in a specific order and to
run automatically in sequence. AWS offers Step Functions, which is a service that lets you
coordinate multiple AWS services into workflows, and this is discussed in the next section.
Visualizing and architecting application components
with AWS Step Functions
AWS Step Functions is an idx_a5f240be orchestration service that you can use to design and build task-
based application workflows. The service uses the concept of states, which represent the
condition of your application at a given point in time while the user interacts with it. While in
a particular state, you can perform specific tasks that define how your application functions.
For example, a state may require calling a Lambda function to process some data.
States idx_8a0fc1f5 can make decisions based on input, perform specified actions, and produce outputs that
are either consumed by other states or bring the application workflow to an end.
States can be any of the following types:
Success or Fail state: Execution idx_9300a7c9 stops with either a success or a idx_f81549d1 failure
Wait state: A idx_fe30d2ad timeout is initiated to allow a process to complete before proceeding to
the next state
Parallel state: The state performs parallel idx_a67bc139 executions – for example, completing an
order fulfillment process while simultaneously sending an email to the customer
Map state: Allows you idx_2a5c10c4 to iterate over a list of items and process each one
Choice state: Chooses idx_c439a530 between branches of execution
Task state: Focuses idx_230cfbfe on carrying out a specified task and may call other AWS services,
such as AWS Lambda, to perform the task
Figure 12.5 illustrates an example idx_2ab42708 of how AWS Step Functions can help you design a workflow
of state machines as a series of event-driven steps.

Chapter 12 360
Figure 12.5: Example Step Functions workflow
In the example illustrated in Figure 12.5, an AWS Step Functions state machine has been
created with the following workflow:
The user starts the app and provides two inputs:
The "operation," which can be either to calculate the area or the circumference
The "value" that the user inputs is the circle's radius (positive integer)
The state machine begins execution at ChooseOperation
ChooseOperation (Choice state)
If operation is "radius", go to CalculateArea
If operation is "circumference", go to CalculateCircumference
CalculateArea (Task state):
Calls the CalculateCircleArea Lambda function
Uses the input value as the radius

chunks.content:
1.2 3.
Lambda returns the area of the circle (π r²)
Execution ends
CalculateCircumference (Task state):
Calls idx_43bbc2a8 the CalculateCircumference Lambda function
Uses the input value as radius
Lambda returns the circumference of the circle (2πr)

AWS Step Functions enables you to build complex distributed application architectures easily
with the help of state machines. You can use the visual interface of the Step Functions
management console, where you drag and drop states, tasks, and define inputs and outputs, or
configure your state machine using idx_92d2a7d7 the Amazon States Language (ASL). This is a simple
JSON-based language used to define workflows in AWS Step Functions.
Finally, there are two types of Step Functions workflows you can create. These are:
Standard workflow: These have idx_75243cec exactly one workflow execution and run for up to 1
year. So, if you have long-running jobs that may also require any human interactions as
a manual approval process, then this workflow type is recommended. You are charged
on a per-state transition basis, and each time a step in your execution is completed.
With standard workflows, you also get execution history and visual debugging.
Express workflow: These are idx_bdfe0b7f for shorter durations up to a maximum of five minutes
and offer at least one workflow execution. Express workflows are ideal for automated
tasks and event rate workflows, such as stream data processing and IoT data ingestion
and processing. Execution history can be sent to CloudWatch logs.
In the next section, you will have the opportunity to gain hands-on experience with the
Amazon EventBridge service to build out a small event-driven solution.
Project task 12 – Notifying an admin when someone
launches an EC2 instance

account. The Belly Brew Co. Limited developers have been granted permissions to launch EC2
instances for development work. However, you want to be notified each time a developer
launches a new EC2 instance.

Review your configuration in the Review and create webpage
Click the Create rule button idx_f09b55d5 at the bottom of the webpage
Now that your EventBridge rule has been configured, you can test out the configuration. In the
next project task, you will launch an EC2 instance and test the EventBridge rule. Because the
rule you created is monitoring any EC2 instances that enter the 'running' state, it should
trigger the SNS notification services, resulting in an email being sent to the email address you
provided in Project Task 12.1.

Chapter 12 366
Project task 12.3 – Launching an EC2 instance
In this project task, you will launch an idx_9fc19677 EC2 instance and test out the EventBridge rule to see if
you get an alert notification in your email.
Here is how you do it:
Ensure you are still logged in to the AWS Management Console
From the search bar at the top of the webpage, search and navigate to EC2
From the left-hand menu, click on Instances
In the right-hand pane, click the Launch instance button
Provide a name for your EC2 instance, such as TestEC2Instance
Next, select Amazon Linux under Quick Start in the Application and OS Images
(Amazon Machine Image)
Select t3.micro from the drop-down list under Instance type
Select Proceed without a key pair (Not recommended) from the drop-down list in
the Key pair (login) section of the webpage
Scroll to the bottom of the webpage and click the Launch instance button. Your EC2
instance will now launch.
From the left-hand menu, click on Instances again to view your instances. Wait for a
few minutes for the instance to launch completely and enter the running state.
Log in to your email account, and you should receive an email confirming that an EC2
instance was idx_a37187ef launched, as shown in Figure 12.9:
Figure 12.9: Email confirming the launch of an EC2 instance and its entry into the running state
In the next project task, you will terminate the resources you created as part of the cleanup
exercise. Since you have now successfully completed the task, there is no requirement to have
the EC2 instances you launched earlier, thereby ensuring you do not incur any unnecessary
usage of your AWS credits (or costs).

chunks.content:
10.11 367 Application Integration
Project task 12.4 – Cleaning up
Now that you have successfully tested out that EventBridge and Amazon SNS can be
configured to send you alerts on any EC2 instance entering a running state, you must
terminate unwanted resources.
Here is how that is done:
While still logged into the AWS Management console and in the EC2 dashboard, click
on Instances from the left-hand menu
In the right-hand pane, select the EC2 instance you launched in Project Task 12.3
Select Terminate (delete) instance from the Instance state drop-down list
In the dialog box that appears, click the Terminate (delete) button, and your EC2
instance will be terminated
From the search bar at the top of the AWS Management Console webpage, search for
and navigate to the EventBridge service
From the left-hand menu, click Rules in the Buses section
In the right-hand pane, select the rule you created earlier in Project Task 12.2 and then
click the Delete button
Confirm that you wish to delete the rule by typing delete in the text box that appears,
and then click the Delete button
The rule will now be deleted
From the search bar at the top of the AWS Management Console webpage, search for
and navigate to Amazon SNS
From the left-hand menu, click on Topics
In the right-hand pane, select the topic you created earlier in Project Task 12.1
Click the Delete button at the top of the webpage
In the dialog box that appears, type in delete me and then click the Delete button
You have now successfully terminated the resources you created in this project. This project
task demonstrated how you can use AWS EventBridge to build event-driven workflows. This
can be particularly useful as part of your overall management of resources, as in the case of this
example. However, you can also use AWS EventBridge for application-level workflows.
Event-driven architectures can be particularly useful to build efficient systems and application
design patterns, ensuring that resources and workloads are only triggered and consumed
when a matching event occurs or at designated schedules.
